A.explanation: Speed stays at zero while force is zero, then rises with constant gradient when force is constant, matching constant acceleration.

B.explanation: A curve with ever-increasing gradient means increasing acceleration, but the force graph shows force becomes constant, not increasing.

C.explanation: A near-vertical jump in speed would need a very large momentary acceleration, and the later flat line would need zero force, which contradicts the constant force shown.

D.explanation: Levelling off at constant speed means acceleration falls to zero, but the force graph stays at a constant positive value.

hints: Notice the force-time graph is zero for a short time and then jumps to a steady constant positive value.
Recall that resultant force sets acceleration through $F = ma$, so the acceleration is also zero and then constant.
Recall that the gradient of a speed-time graph equals acceleration, so link zero acceleration to a flat line and constant acceleration to a straight sloping line.
walkthrough: The force graph shows $F = 0$ from $t = 0$ until the accelerator is pressed, then $F$ jumps to a constant positive value and stays there.
Use $F = ma$ with constant mass $m$. So acceleration $a = F/m$ is first zero and then a constant positive value.
On a speed-time graph, gradient $= a = \Delta v / \Delta t$. Zero acceleration means zero gradient, so speed remains $0$ while the car is stationary.
After the jump, constant positive $a$ means constant positive gradient, so speed increases linearly with time as $v = u + at$ with $u = 0$.
Only the graph that is flat at zero and then a straight line of constant slope matches this, and This is option A.
